question: The consequences of the Houthi attacks in the Red Sea are numerous, with the shipping industry being hit particularly hard. In addition to their rising fuel and insurance bills, companies are seeing an increase in the cost of carbon offsets as a result of the long detours they have to make.

Since 1 January 2024, all commercial and passenger ships of more than 5 000 gross tonnes sailing to or from EU ports have been subject to the emissions trading system, meaning they have to offset 40 % of their CO2 emissions. This increase in costs, as well as being permanent, is compounded by the exceptional security situation.

Companies are also being penalised for emitting more CO2 because vessels are having to sail faster in an effort to make up for the longer journey times. The additional costs incurred as a result of these penalties are passed on to customers and ultimately to consumers. They are also causing congestion in major ports, in an already very tense economic environment.
As a result, what measures does the Commission intend to take to ease the pressure on the operators concerned and exempt them from the costs associated with carbon quotas?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.4.2024) While maritime transport plays an essential role in the EU economy, it is also a large and growing source of greenhouse emissions. In 2021, ships calling at EU ports emitted 124 million tonnes of CO2. Under the European Green Deal, action has been taken to reduce these emissions.

The rules to report CO2 emissions by shipping companies under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive1 are defined in Regulation (EU) 2015/7572. According to these rules, it is not possible to exempt emissions from ships deviating from their scheduled or usual route due to security situations. Similarly, the ETS Directive does not provide for specific exemptions under such circumstances.
However, the EU has recently taken swift action to contribute to restoring and safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea3.

In addition, the possible effect of rerouting on ETS compliance costs for shipping companies will be attenuated by the phase-in approach, since shipping companies will have to surrender allowances for only 20%4 of their 2024 emissions in relation to voyages starting or ending outside of the EU.
1 Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 October 2003 establishing a system

for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Union and amending Council Directive 96/61/EC (OJ L 275, 25.10.2003, p. 32). 2 Regulation (EU) 2015/757 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2015 on the monitoring, reporting and verification of greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport, and amending Directive 2009/16/EC. 3 https://www.consilium.europa.
